## The AI race is actually a context race


For the last decade, the corporate mantra has been simple: collect more data. Businesses built massive data lakes, tracked every click, and hoarded customer touchpoints like digital gold.


But we didn’t build a treasure trove. We created an ocean—and lost sight of the shore.


Today, businesses aren't suffering from a lack of data. They're overwhelmed by too much disconnected data. Add in the proliferation of channels like WhatsApp, RCS, and social media, and the problem only compounds.


We have plenty of information. What we lack is context.


That helps explain why[99% of companies](https://www.twilio.com/en-us/report/navigating-data-deluge-charting-customer-context) say they face major challenges that prevent them from truly understanding their customers. The chief obstacle?[Connecting customer data](https://www.twilio.com/en-us/report/navigating-data-deluge-charting-customer-context) across channels like voice, email, and messaging (48%).


That disconnect was frustrating before AI. Now, it's a fundamental barrier to delivering the intelligent experiences brands are racing to build.


To succeed in the AI era, leaders need to shift their focus. The race is no longer about who can collect the most data. It's about who can connect it—and turn it into context that humans and AI can actually use.


## Customer context requires a new architecture


A purchase history tells you what someone bought. A support transcript tells you what went wrong. Website behavior tells you what they browsed. But none of those data points, on their own, tell you who your customer is or what they need right now.


That's the difference between customer data and customer context.


Unlocking that context requires an architecture that doesn't just collect signals, but connects, interprets, and activates them. Think of it as four interconnected layers:


1.


**The data layer connects the signals.** Customer information needs to flow across systems and channels rather than remaining trapped inside individual applications. That means bringing together behavioral, transactional, demographic, and conversational data together in one place.


2.


**The semantic layer gives those signals meaning.** Connecting customer behavior with history, preferences, and intent creates a clearer understanding of who someone is, what they're trying to accomplish, and what they might need next.


3.


**The application layer turns context into action.** With that understanding, businesses can create more relevant journeys across marketing, sales, and support—whether that's a personalized product recommendation, a timely offer, or simply picking up where the last interaction left off.


4.


**The AI layer makes context usable at scale.** AI can synthesize enormous amounts of information, detect intent and sentiment, surface relevant knowledge, and determine appropriate next steps faster than humans could do manually. But its effectiveness depends entirely on the layers beneath it.


And the order matters. Putting sophisticated AI on top of disconnected data doesn't magically create customer understanding. It simply lets businesses act on incomplete information faster.


## AI makes context more valuable — and more urgent


AI dramatically increases what businesses can do with customer data. But it also raises the stakes when that data is incomplete.


An AI agent might be capable of responding instantly, reasoning through a problem, or recommending the next best action. But if it can't see that a customer already contacted support yesterday, just received a replacement product, or has explained the same problem three times, that intelligence only goes so far.


And there's a striking disconnect between how brands think they're doing and what customers actually experience. While[84% of brands](https://www.twilio.com/en-us/report/navigating-data-deluge-charting-customer-context) say their AI agents recognize returning customers and access their history effectively, 74% of consumers say they've had to repeat themselves when interacting with an AI assistant. When they're handed off to a human, 76% say the agent has little or no context about their issue—forcing them to repeat themselves yet again.


Customers aren't grading AI on its technical sophistication. They're judging the experience: Did you understand me? Did you remember me? Did you solve my problem?


That's why the next phase of AI won't be won by the company with the flashiest chatbot. The advantage will come from giving AI—and the humans working alongside it—the right context at the right moment.


## What context looks like in action


Twilio has seen what happens when connected context is put into action. Using Twilio Segment, our team built a unified data foundation that powers our AI Inbound Sales Assistant, ISA. She supports prospects however they choose to get started—answering questions and connecting those who want to speak with sales, while identifying and addressing friction for those completing sign-up on their own.


Today, ISA supports 100% of new Twilio sign-ups and 95% of inbound sales inquiries, responding 25X faster when customers ask to speak with sales. Across roughly 4,800 monthly inbound sales conversations, she maintains an average customer satisfaction score of 4.7 out of 5.


That positive experience also translates into business results. Customers who interact with ISA upgrade at 3X the rate of those who don't, and reengaging abandoned sign-ups has generated 11,600 additional customer sign-ups and nearly $4 million in additional closed-won business.


It’s a powerful example of what becomes possible when customer data isn't simply stored, but connected, understood, and put to work.


## From a 360-degree view to real-time understanding


For years, the goal was to create a 360-degree view of the customer. AI gives businesses the opportunity to do something far more valuable: act on that view in real time.


The companies that stand out won't necessarily be the ones sitting on the largest stores of customer information. They'll be the ones that can turn fragmented signals into context, context into intelligence, and intelligence into action.


Because in the AI era, more data isn't the competitive advantage.


Knowing what to do with it is.
